title: Domestication
paras: Domestication is a multi-generational mutualistic relationship in which an animal species takes over control and care of another organism's development to obtain from the latter a steady supply of resources — typically food — while the latter often also benefits and coevolve from such interspecific relationship via reciprocal provision of nutrients (e.g. via feeds), sheltering and protection. The process is gradual and geographically diffuse, based on trial and error. In animals, domestication affects genes for behavior, making them less territorial and aggressive; in plants, domestication affects genes for morphology, such as increasing seed size and stopping the shattering of cereal seedheads. Such changes both make the domesticated organisms easier to handle for the host, and conversely also reduce their ability to survive in the wild.

The most prominent example of domestication is that by modern humans (Homo sapiens sapiens), who have systematically developed taming and artificial breeding of various terrestrial/aquatic animals (known collectively as livestock) and plants (known as crops and cultivars) for harvesting food (e.g. meat, eggs, milk, honey, grains, fruits, vegetables and seeds/beans), to procure various useful animal products (e.g. hides and leather, furs and feathers, fats and oils, waxes and silk) and plant products (e.g. fibers, herbs, fodders and timbers), as well as to provide labor, service, emotional support/companionship and ornamental values. Some of these domesticated species have even become synanthropic and largely lost the ability to survive ferally in the wild.
